questions.question: Given $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right)$, the expression that equals $(\bar z)^{-1}$ is
questions.answer: $\bar z=2\left(\cos\frac\pi3-i\sin\frac\pi3\right)=2\,\mathrm{cis}\left(-\frac\pi3\right)$. By de Moivre's theorem, $(\bar z)^{-1}=\frac12\mathrm{cis}\left(\frac\pi3\right)=\frac12\left(\cos\frac\pi3+i\sin\frac\pi3\right)$ (C).

questions.question: Which of the following is a primitive of $\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\tan^4x}$?
questions.answer: $\displaystyle\int\sec^2x(\tan x)^{-4}dx=\frac{(\tan x)^{-3}}{-3}+C=-\frac13\cot^3x+C$ (B).

questions.question: One of the complex solutions to $z^5=-a$, where $a$ is a positive real constant, is $a^{\frac15}\mathrm{cis}\left(\dfrac\pi5\right)$. One of the other solutions is a real number and is equal to
questions.answer: The five roots are equally spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{5}$. Adding $2\times\frac{2\pi}5=\frac{4\pi}5$ to $\frac\pi5$ gives $\pi$, so the real root is $a^{\frac15}\mathrm{cis}\,\pi=-a^{\frac15}$ (B). (Indeed $(-a^{1/5})^5=-a$.)

questions.question: If $\dfrac{4}{(2x-1)(3-x)}=\dfrac{A}{2x-1}+\dfrac{B}{3-x}$, then $A$ and $B$ have values of:
If $\omega$ is the complex cube root of unity, then the value of $\left(1-3\omega+\omega^2\right)\left(1+\omega-8\omega^2\right)$ is:
questions.answer: Since $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$: $1+\omega^2=-\omega$, so $1-3\omega+\omega^2=-4\omega$; and $1+\omega=-\omega^2$, so $1+\omega-8\omega^2=-9\omega^2$. The product is $36\omega^3=36$ since $\omega^3=1$ (D).

questions.question: The sign on a fence reads "If you are not authorised, you may not enter." Which of the following statements is logically equivalent to the one above?
questions.answer: An implication is equivalent to its contrapositive. The contrapositive of "if not authorised then may not enter" is "if you may enter then you are authorised" (A). B and D are the inverse and converse.
options: If you may enter, then you are authorised.
If you are authorised, then you may enter.
If you are not authorised, then you may enter.
If you may not enter, then you are not authorised.

questions.question: $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are three collinear points with position vectors $\underset{\sim}{p}$, $\underset{\sim}{q}$ and $\underset{\sim}{r}$ respectively, where $Q$ lies between $P$ and $R$. If $|\overrightarrow{QR}|=\frac12|\overrightarrow{PQ}|$, then $\underset{\sim}{r}$ is equal to
questions.answer: $Q$ lies between $P$ and $R$, so $\overrightarrow{QR}=\frac12\overrightarrow{PQ}$. Then $\underset{\sim}{r}=\underset{\sim}{q}+\frac12\left(\underset{\sim}{q}-\underset{\sim}{p}\right)=\frac32\underset{\sim}{q}-\frac12\underset{\sim}{p}$ (A).

questions.question: Suppose that $x+\dfrac1x=-1$. What is the value of $x^{2025}+\dfrac{1}{x^{2025}}$?
Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{14+6x-x^2}}$.
questions.answer: Complete the square: $14+6x-x^2=23-(x-3)^2$. So $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{23-(x-3)^2}}=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x-3}{\sqrt{23}}\right)+C$.

questions.question: Express $-1+\sqrt3\,i$ in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer: $|{-1}+\sqrt3 i|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$. The point is in the second quadrant with $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{1}\right)=\frac\pi3$ as the related angle, so $\arg=\pi-\frac\pi3=\frac{2\pi}3$. Hence $-1+\sqrt3i=2\,\mathrm{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}3\right)$.

questions.question: Given $-1+\sqrt3\,i=2\,\mathrm{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}3\right)$, evaluate $\left(-1+\sqrt3\,i\right)^{-6}$.
questions.answer: By de Moivre's theorem, $\left(2\,\mathrm{cis}\frac{2\pi}3\right)^{-6}=2^{-6}\mathrm{cis}(-4\pi)=\dfrac1{64}\left(\cos4\pi-i\sin4\pi\right)=\dfrac1{64}$.

questions.question: State whether $\left(-1+\sqrt3\,i\right)^n$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, is purely imaginary. Justify.
questions.answer: It is never purely imaginary. $\left(-1+\sqrt3i\right)^n=2^n\mathrm{cis}\left(\frac{2n\pi}3\right)$. For this to be purely imaginary we need $\frac{2n\pi}3=\frac{(2k+1)\pi}2$ for some integer $k$, i.e. $4n=3(2k+1)$, so $4n=6k+3$. The left side is even and the right side is odd, which is impossible for integers $n$ and $k$. Hence $\left(-1+\sqrt3i\right)^n$ is not purely imaginary for any integer $n$.

questions.question: Express $e^{1-\frac{i\pi}{6}}$ in Cartesian form.
questions.answer: $e^{1-\frac{i\pi}6}=e\cdot e^{-\frac{i\pi}6}=e\left(\cos\frac\pi6-i\sin\frac\pi6\right)=e\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2-\frac12i\right)=\dfrac e2\left(\sqrt3-i\right)$.

questions.question: Consider the following statements about a polynomial $P(x)$. (i) If $P(x)$ is even, then $P'(x)$ is odd. (ii) If $P'(x)$ is even, then $P(x)$ is odd. Indicate whether each of these statements is true or false. Give reasons for your answers.
questions.answer:
(i) True. If $P(x)$ is even, it contains only even powers: $P(x)=a_nx^{2n}+a_{n-1}x^{2n-2}+\cdots+a_2x^2+a_0$. Then $P'(x)=2na_nx^{2n-1}+(2n-2)a_{n-1}x^{2n-3}+\cdots+2a_2x$ has only odd powers, so $P'(x)$ is odd.

(ii) False. If $P'(x)$ is even, then $P(x)$ is a sum of odd powers plus a constant of integration $C$. The constant (an even term) need not be zero. Counterexample: $P(x)=x^3+1$ has $P'(x)=3x^2$ (even), but $P(-x)=-x^3+1
eq-P(x)$, so $P$ is not odd.

questions.question: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ to find $\displaystyle\int\frac{15}{17+8\cos x}\,dx$.
questions.answer: With $\cos x=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$: $\displaystyle\int\frac{15}{17+8\cos x}dx=\int\frac{15\cdot2}{17(1+t^2)+8(1-t^2)}dt=\int\frac{30}{25+9t^2}dt=\frac{30}{9}\int\frac{dt}{t^2+\frac{25}9}$. This is $\dfrac{30}{9}\cdot\dfrac35\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3t}5\right)=2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3t}{5}\right)+C$. So the integral is $2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac35\tan\dfrac x2\right)+C$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x-5}{x^2+2x+2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Write $2x-5=(2x+2)-7$. Then $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+2}{x^2+2x+2}dx-7\int\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2+1}=\ln\left(x^2+2x+2\right)-7\tan^{-1}(x+1)+C$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int x^3\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Let $u=4-x^2$, so $x^2=4-u$ and $x\,dx=-\frac12du$. Then $\displaystyle\int x^2\sqrt{4-x^2}\,x\,dx=-\frac12\int(4-u)u^{1/2}du=-\frac12\left(\frac83u^{3/2}-\frac25u^{5/2}\right)+C=-\frac43u^{3/2}+\frac15u^{5/2}+C$. So the integral is $-\frac43(4-x^2)^{3/2}+\frac15(4-x^2)^{5/2}+C$.

questions.question: The vertices of a triangle $ABC$ are defined by the position vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-6\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-4\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-4\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Show that $\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac12$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}$. $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt6$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt6$, $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=-2+4+4=6$. So $\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt6\cdot2\sqrt6}=\dfrac{6}{12}=\dfrac12$.

questions.question: In triangle $ABC$ with $A(1,-6,-2)$, $B(0,-4,-1)$, $C(3,-4,2)$, $AB=\sqrt6$, $AC=2\sqrt6$ and $\cos\angle BAC=\frac12$. Hence find the exact area of triangle $ABC$.
questions.answer: $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. Area $=\frac12(AB)(AC)\sin60^\circ=\frac12\cdot\sqrt6\cdot2\sqrt6\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=3\sqrt3$ square units.

questions.question: Consider the point $P(2,1,-6)$ and the line $L$ with equation $\underset{\sim}{r}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the line.
questions.answer: A general point on $L$ is $A(-1+t,\,2+3t,\,1+2t)$, so $\overrightarrow{PA}=\begin{pmatrix}t-3\\3t+1\\2t+7\end{pmatrix}$. The shortest distance occurs when $\overrightarrow{PA}\perp$ the direction $\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}$: $(t-3)+3(3t+1)+2(2t+7)=14t+14=0$, so $t=-1$. Then $\overrightarrow{PA}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and the distance is $\sqrt{16+4+25}=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt5$ units.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that if $a$ and $b$ are both positive integers then $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba\ge2$.
questions.answer: Suppose, for contradiction, that $a,b$ are positive integers with $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba<2$. Multiplying by $ab>0$: $a^2+b^2<2ab$, so $a^2-2ab+b^2<0$, i.e. $(a-b)^2<0$. This is impossible since the square of a real number is never negative. Hence the assumption is false, and $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba\ge2$.

questions.question: The line $L_1$ has vector equation $\underset{\sim}{r}_1=6\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}+7\underset{\sim}{k}+\lambda\left(3\underset{\sim}{i}+4\underset{\sim}{j}+5\underset{\sim}{k}\right)$. The line $L_2$ has vector equation $\underset{\sim}{r}_2=7\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}+4\underset{\sim}{k}+\mu\left(2\underset{\sim}{i}+\underset{\sim}{j}+\underset{\sim}{k}\right)$. Determine whether the two lines are parallel.
questions.answer: The direction vectors $(3,4,5)$ and $(2,1,1)$ are not scalar multiples of each other, so the lines are not parallel.

questions.question: The line $L_1$ is $\underset{\sim}{r}_1=(6,5,7)+\lambda(3,4,5)$ and $L_2$ is $\underset{\sim}{r}_2=(7,3,4)+\mu(2,1,1)$. Determine whether the two lines intersect and, if so, where they intersect.
questions.answer: Equate components: $6+3\lambda=7+2\mu$, $5+4\lambda=3+\mu$, $7+5\lambda=4+\mu$. From the last two: $\mu=4\lambda+2=5\lambda+3$, so $\lambda=-1$ and $\mu=-2$. Check in the first: $6-3=3$ and $7-4=3$ ✓. The lines intersect at $(3,1,2)$.

questions.question: The line $L_1$ is $(6,5,7)+\lambda(3,4,5)$ and $L_2$ is $(7,3,4)+\mu(2,1,1)$, and they intersect at $(3,1,2)$. Determine whether the two lines are skew.
questions.answer: Skew lines are not parallel and do not intersect. These lines intersect, so they are not skew.

questions.question: The line $L_1$ has direction $(3,4,5)$ and $L_2$ has direction $(2,1,1)$. Determine whether the two lines are perpendicular.
questions.answer: $(3,4,5)\cdot(2,1,1)=6+4+5=15\neq0$, so the lines are not perpendicular.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\sec^3x\,dx$.
questions.answer: Integrate by parts with $u=\sec x$, $dv=\sec^2x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int\sec^3x\,dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec x\tan^2x\,dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec x(\sec^2x-1)dx=\sec x\tan x-\int\sec^3x\,dx+\int\sec x\,dx$. So $2\int\sec^3x\,dx=\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|$ and $\displaystyle\int\sec^3x\,dx=\frac12\left(\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|\right)+C$.

questions.question: Sketch the region where the inequalities $-\dfrac\pi2\le\arg(z-1-2i)\le\dfrac\pi4$ and $|z|\le\sqrt5$ both hold.
questions.answer: $\arg(z-(1+2i))$ is the angle of the ray from the point $(1,2)$. The condition $-\frac\pi2\le\arg\le\frac\pi4$ describes the sector between the downward vertical ray from $(1,2)$ and the ray at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal (the line $y=x+1$), i.e. the region with $x\ge1$ and $y\le x+1$. The condition $|z|\le\sqrt5$ is the disc of radius $\sqrt5$ centred at the origin; $(1,2)$ lies on its boundary. The $45^\circ$ ray immediately leaves the disc, so the region is the part of the disc to the right of the line $x=1$ (a circular segment, bounded by the chord from $(1,-2)$ to $(1,2)$ and the arc through $(\sqrt5,0)$). See the diagram.

questions.question: Let $P$ be the proposition: if $k+1$ is divisible by 3, then $k^3+1$ is divisible by 3, $k\in\mathbb Z^+$. Write down the converse of the proposition $P$ and state, with reasons, whether this converse is true or false.
questions.answer: Converse: if $k^3+1$ is divisible by 3, then $k+1$ is divisible by 3. This is true. Since $k^3+1=(k+1)\left(k^2-k+1\right)$, consider $k$ modulo 3. If $k\equiv0$: $k^3+1\equiv1$; if $k\equiv1$: $k^3+1\equiv2$; if $k\equiv2$: $k^3+1\equiv9\equiv0$ and $k+1\equiv0$. So $k^3+1$ is divisible by 3 only when $k\equiv2\pmod3$, i.e. exactly when $k+1$ is divisible by 3. Hence the converse is true.

questions.question: Given that $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2a_n}$ and $a_1=1$, prove by mathematical induction that for all integers $n\ge1$, $a_n=2^{\left(1-2^{(1-n)}\right)}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1** ($n=1$): $a_1=2^{1-2^0}=2^0=1$, which agrees with $a_1=1$. True for $n=1$.

**Step 2:** Assume true for $n=k$: $a_k=2^{1-2^{1-k}}$.

**Step 3:** Prove for $n=k+1$, i.e. $a_{k+1}=2^{1-2^{-k}}$. $a_{k+1}=\sqrt{2a_k}=\left(2\cdot2^{1-2^{1-k}}ight)^{ rac12}=\left(2^{2-2^{1-k}}ight)^{ rac12}=2^{1- rac12\cdot2^{1-k}}=2^{1-2^{-k}}=2^{1-2^{1-(k+1)}}$.

**Step 4:** True for $n=1$, and if true for $n=k$ then true for $n=k+1$, so by mathematical induction it is true for all integers $n\ge1$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\cos^5x\,dx$.
questions.answer: $\cos^5x=\cos x\left(1-\sin^2x\right)^2$. Let $u=\sin x$: $\displaystyle\int\left(1-u^2\right)^2du=\int\left(1-2u^2+u^4\right)du=u-\frac23u^3+\frac15u^5+C$. So $\displaystyle\int\cos^5x\,dx=\sin x-\frac23\sin^3x+\frac15\sin^5x+C$.

questions.question: Find the points of intersection of the line $\underset{\sim}{r}=t\left(4\underset{\sim}{i}-2\underset{\sim}{j}-5\underset{\sim}{k}\right)$ and the sphere which has equation $x^2+y^2+z^2=90$.
questions.answer: On the line, $x=4t$, $y=-2t$, $z=-5t$. Substituting: $16t^2+4t^2+25t^2=90$, so $45t^2=90$ and $t=\pm\sqrt2$. The points of intersection are $\left(4\sqrt2,\,-2\sqrt2,\,-5\sqrt2\right)$ and $\left(-4\sqrt2,\,2\sqrt2,\,5\sqrt2\right)$.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^nx\,dx$, where $n$ is an integer and $n\ge3$. Show that $I_n+I_{n-2}=\dfrac1{n-1}$.
questions.answer: $I_n+I_{n-2}=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\left(\tan^2x+1\right)dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\sec^2x\,dx=\left[\frac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1}\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\frac1{n-1}-0=\frac1{n-1}$.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^nx\,dx$ and $I_n+I_{n-2}=\dfrac1{n-1}$ for $n\ge3$. Hence evaluate $I_5$.
questions.answer: $I_5+I_3=\frac14$ and $I_3+I_1=\frac12$. Subtracting: $I_5=\frac14-\frac12+I_1=-\frac14+I_1$. $I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,dx=\left[\ln|\sec x|\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\ln\sqrt2=\frac12\ln2$. So $I_5=\dfrac12\ln2-\dfrac14$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{(2x+1)(x-3)^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Let $\dfrac{x}{(2x+1)(x-3)^2}=\dfrac{A}{2x+1}+\dfrac{B}{x-3}+\dfrac{C}{(x-3)^2}$, so $x=A(x-3)^2+B(2x+1)(x-3)+C(2x+1)$. Let $x=3$: $3=7C$, so $C=\frac37$. Let $x=-\frac12$: $-\frac12=\frac{49}4A$, so $A=-\frac2{49}$. Comparing $x^2$ coefficients: $0=A+2B$, so $B=\frac1{49}$. Then $\displaystyle\int\left(-\frac{2}{49(2x+1)}+\frac{1}{49(x-3)}+\frac{3}{7(x-3)^2}\right)dx=-\frac1{49}\ln|2x+1|+\frac1{49}\ln|x-3|-\frac{3}{7(x-3)}+C$, i.e. $\dfrac1{49}\ln\left|\dfrac{x-3}{2x+1}\right|-\dfrac3{7(x-3)}+C$.

questions.question: Find an expression for $\cot2\theta$ in terms of $\tan\theta$.
questions.answer: $\tan2\theta=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}$, so $\cot2\theta=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{2\tan\theta}$.

questions.question: Show that $\tan\theta$ and $-\cot\theta$ satisfy the equation $x^2+2x\cot2\theta-1=0$.
questions.answer: The sum of the two numbers is $\tan\theta-\cot\theta=\dfrac{\tan^2\theta-1}{\tan\theta}=-2\cdot\dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{2\tan\theta}=-2\cot2\theta$, and their product is $\tan\theta\cdot(-\cot\theta)=-1$. A quadratic with sum of roots $-2\cot2\theta$ and product $-1$ is $x^2-(\text{sum})x+\text{product}=x^2+2x\cot2\theta-1=0$. So $\tan\theta$ and $-\cot\theta$ are its roots.

questions.question: Given that $\tan\theta$ and $-\cot\theta$ satisfy $x^2+2x\cot2\theta-1=0$, hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac\pi8$.
questions.answer: Let $\theta=\frac\pi8$: $x^2+2x\cot\frac\pi4-1=0$, i.e. $x^2+2x-1=0$. Then $(x+1)^2=2$ and $x=-1\pm\sqrt2$. $\tan\frac\pi8>0$ and $-\cot\frac\pi8<0$ are the two roots, so $\tan\frac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$ (and $-\cot\frac\pi8=-\sqrt2-1$).

questions.question: Using $\tan\theta$ and $-\cot\theta$ as roots of $x^2+2x\cot2\theta-1=0$ and $\cot\dfrac\pi8=\sqrt2+1$, hence find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac\pi{16}-\cot\dfrac\pi{16}$.
questions.answer: With $\theta=\frac\pi{16}$, the roots of $x^2+2x\cot\frac\pi8-1=0$ are $\tan\frac\pi{16}$ and $-\cot\frac\pi{16}$. Their sum is $\tan\frac\pi{16}-\cot\frac\pi{16}=-2\cot\frac\pi8=-2\left(\sqrt2+1\right)=-2\sqrt2-2$.

questions.question: In $\triangle OAB$, $BC$ is the altitude from $B$ to $OA$ and $AD$ is the altitude from $A$ to $OB$. $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $OA$ and $OB$ respectively. $\overrightarrow{OA}=\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\underset{\sim}{b}$. Use vector methods to show that $|\overrightarrow{OM}||\overrightarrow{OC}|=|\overrightarrow{ON}||\overrightarrow{OD}|$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{OC}$ is the projection of $\underset{\sim}{b}$ onto $\underset{\sim}{a}$, so $|\overrightarrow{OC}|=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}|}$ (for an acute angle $O$). Also $|\overrightarrow{OM}|=\frac12|\underset{\sim}{a}|$. Hence $|\overrightarrow{OM}||\overrightarrow{OC}|=\frac12|\underset{\sim}{a}|\cdot\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}|}=\frac12\,\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}$. Similarly $\overrightarrow{OD}$ is the projection of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ onto $\underset{\sim}{b}$, so $|\overrightarrow{OD}|=\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{b}|}$ and $|\overrightarrow{ON}|=\frac12|\underset{\sim}{b}|$, giving $|\overrightarrow{ON}||\overrightarrow{OD}|=\frac12\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}$. The two products are equal.

questions.question: In $\triangle OAB$, the altitudes $BC$ (from $B$ to $OA$) and $AD$ (from $A$ to $OB$) meet at $E$. A line drawn from $O$ passes through $E$ to meet the side $BA$ at point $F$. By letting $\overrightarrow{OE}=\underset{\sim}{e}$, prove that $\overrightarrow{OF}\perp\overrightarrow{BA}$.
questions.answer: $BE\perp OA$, so $\left(\underset{\sim}{e}-\underset{\sim}{b}\right)\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=0$, giving $\underset{\sim}{e}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}$. $AE\perp OB$, so $\left(\underset{\sim}{e}-\underset{\sim}{a}\right)\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=0$, giving $\underset{\sim}{e}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}$. Hence $\underset{\sim}{e}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}=\underset{\sim}{e}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}$, so $\underset{\sim}{e}\cdot\left(\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}\right)=0$, i.e. $\overrightarrow{OE}\perp\overrightarrow{AB}$. Since $O$, $E$, $F$ are collinear, $\overrightarrow{OF}$ is parallel to $\overrightarrow{OE}$, so $\overrightarrow{OF}\perp\overrightarrow{BA}$.

questions.question: Using mathematical induction, prove that for $n\ge2$, where $n$ is an integer, $1+\dfrac12+\dfrac13+\cdots+\dfrac1n>\dfrac{2n}{n+1}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1** ($n=2$): LHS $=1+ rac12= rac32$ and RHS $= rac43$. Since $ rac32> rac43$, true for $n=2$.

**Step 2:** Assume true for $n=k$ ($k\ge2$): $1+ rac12+\cdots+ rac1k> rac{2k}{k+1}$.

**Step 3:** Prove for $n=k+1$: $1+\cdots+ rac1k+ rac1{k+1}> rac{2k}{k+1}+ rac1{k+1}= rac{2k+1}{k+1}$ (by the assumption). It remains to show $ rac{2k+1}{k+1}\ge rac{2(k+1)}{k+2}$: $(2k+1)(k+2)-2(k+1)^2=2k^2+5k+2-2k^2-4k-2=k>0$, so $ rac{2k+1}{k+1}> rac{2(k+1)}{k+2}$. Hence the sum $> rac{2(k+1)}{(k+1)+1}$.

**Step 4:** By mathematical induction the result is true for all integers $n\ge2$.

questions.question: For positive real numbers $a,b$ and $c$, where $a\ne b\ne c$, prove $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$.
questions.answer: $a^3+b^3-ab(a+b)=a^3+b^3-a^2b-ab^2=a^2(a-b)-b^2(a-b)=(a-b)\left(a^2-b^2\right)=(a-b)^2(a+b)$. Since $a\neq b$, $(a-b)^2>0$, and $a+b>0$, so the expression is positive. Hence $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$.

questions.question: For positive real numbers $a,b$ and $c$ with $a\ne b\ne c$, given $a^3+b^3>ab(a+b)$ (and similarly for the other pairs), hence or otherwise prove that $2\left(a^3+b^3+c^3\right)>a^2(b+c)+b^2(a+c)+c^2(a+b)$.
questions.answer: Applying the result to each pair: $a^3+b^3>a^2b+ab^2$, $b^3+c^3>b^2c+bc^2$ and $a^3+c^3>a^2c+ac^2$. Adding: $2\left(a^3+b^3+c^3\right)>a^2b+ab^2+b^2c+bc^2+a^2c+ac^2=a^2(b+c)+b^2(a+c)+c^2(a+b)$.

questions.question: The function $F(p)$ is defined as $F(p)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^tx^{p-1}e^{-x}\,dx$, for $p>0$. Show that $F(1)=1$.
questions.answer: $F(1)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^te^{-x}dx=\lim_{t\to\infty}\left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^t=\lim_{t\to\infty}\left(1-e^{-t}\right)=1$.

questions.question: The function $F(p)$ is defined as $F(p)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^tx^{p-1}e^{-x}\,dx$, for $p>0$. Use integration by parts to show that $F(p+1)=p\times F(p)$.
questions.answer: $F(p+1)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^tx^pe^{-x}dx$. By parts with $u=x^p$, $dv=e^{-x}dx$: $\displaystyle\int_0^tx^pe^{-x}dx=\left[-x^pe^{-x}\right]_0^t+p\int_0^tx^{p-1}e^{-x}dx=-t^pe^{-t}+p\int_0^tx^{p-1}e^{-x}dx$. As $t\to\infty$, $t^pe^{-t}\to0$ (the exponential dominates), so $F(p+1)=p\,F(p)$.

questions.question: Given $F(1)=1$ and $F(p+1)=p\,F(p)$, where $F(p)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^tx^{p-1}e^{-x}dx$, hence find $F(n)$ for integers $n\ge1$.
questions.answer: $F(2)=1\cdot F(1)=1$, $F(3)=2F(2)=2$, $F(4)=3F(3)=6$, and in general $F(n+1)=nF(n)$, so $F(n)=(n-1)(n-2)\cdots2\cdot1\cdot F(1)=(n-1)!$. (This is proved formally by induction on $n$.)
